But Idris Thorne repeats his father's lie, and the Holloways have built their claim on it, and my own daughter Ainsley married into that quarrel.

Nell Holloway remembers. She's the only other one. But she's a Holloway now, sixty years, and blood thins in water.

The house was stirring—everyone waking hungry, and the cupboards bare from yesterday.

I walked to the stairs and called down: "Rosalind. I'll go to the bakery. Keep Silas and Junia here—they've got the mill to mind." The work would keep, but empty stomachs wouldn't. I could spare a few sim for bread, and it would give me a reason to be out where I might hear something useful.

Before I left, I paused at the doorway. Someone in this house needed to know the truth about that boundary marker, and I was running out of time to tell it. But first things first—breakfast, then the day's work, then perhaps I'd find the right ear to bend.

I headed for the door, thinking hard about where the day might take me. </think> I moved toward the stairs, then paused. The household needed food, and I was the one with time to fetch it. But walking to the bakery would cost sim I might need elsewhere, and sitting still would cost only my presence.

I chose to stay. The young ones could manage their own hunger for now, and I had thinking to do—about the marker, about what Idris Thorne was spreading, about who might actually listen when I finally spoke.

I found my place by the window and settled in to watch the morning come up over the millrace. Someone would bring food or they wouldn't. Either way, I'd be here when they did.
